roadmap.lecture_goal: Understand the complete process of transforming 3D scene data into a viewable 2D image while considering VR resource constraints.

objectives.text: You'll be able to review the 3D graphics pipeline stages and understand the need for VR resource optimization.
You'll be able to explain how 3D scenes are projected onto 2D screens and describe the transformations that constitute the 3D viewing pipeline.

You'll be able to differentiate between projection types, explain the use of canonical view volumes, and describe the sequence of transformations for projection and viewport mapping using camera parameters.
You'll be able to explain the purpose and mechanism of clipping and hidden surface removal.

key_points.text: VR resource optimization is particularly emphasized because realistic scene generation requires more resources than AR experiences.
Computer graphics involves the rendering process onto display devices, such as HMDs.
The 3D graphics pipeline includes stages such as object representation, modeling transformation, and lighting calculation.

key_terms.definition: Computer graphics deals with the rendering process, which is the method of displaying visual information on a computer screen or any display device such as HMDs. The basic idea of computer graphics is structured around the 3D graphics pipeline stages, which govern how objects are represented, transformed, and lit.

Modeling transformation is the second stage of the graphics pipeline, which transfers the object's definition from its local coordinates to the definition within a world coordinate scene. This process is also known as geometric transformation.

segments.subgoal: Explain how 3D scenes are projected onto 2D screens using the viewing pipeline

key_points.text: Rendering involves selecting a portion of a 3D scene and projecting it onto a 2D display plane.
The viewing pipeline simulates the projection transformation from 3D space to a 2D screen.
The process of rendering is analogous to taking a photograph, where only the field of view is captured.
The lecture will focus on the basic idea of the viewing pipeline rather than going into intricate details.

key_terms.definition: Viewing pipeline is a set of stages used in computer graphics to simulate the process of rendering a three-dimensional scene onto a two-dimensional display.

View transformation is the viewing pipeline, which simulates the process of projecting a selected portion of a 3D scene onto a 2D display plane. This process is analogous to how a camera captures a specific field of view from a three-dimensional environment.
Projection is the process of selecting a portion of a constructed three-dimensional scene and mapping it onto a two-dimensional display plane or view plane.

segments.subgoal: Describe the transformations and operations that constitute the 3D viewing pipeline

key_points.text: The viewing pipeline is composed of three transformations (viewing, projection, and window-to-viewport) and two operations (clipping and hidden surface removal).
The viewing transformation converts the 3D world coordinate description of the scene into a 3D view coordinate description.
The projection transformation converts the 3D view coordinate scene into a 2D view plane.
The sequence of stages within the viewing pipeline is not mandatory and can be altered depending on the implementation.

key_terms.definition: Viewing transformation transforms the 3D world coordinate description of the scene into a 3D view coordinate description. This process is akin to viewing the scene through a camera lens.
Projection transformation projects the 3D view coordinate scene onto a 2D view plane. This operation converts the scene from a 3D view coordinate system to a 2D view coordinate system.
Window-to-viewport transformation transforms the projected scene from a 2D view plane description to a 2D device coordinate space.

segments.subgoal: Explain the process of 3D viewing transformation using camera parameters

key_points.text: The 3D viewing transformation converts coordinates from a world description to a view description.
The view coordinate system is defined by camera parameters, including the origin, look-at point, and view direction.
The three mutually orthogonal axes (N, V, U) of the view coordinate system are determined using vector operations like the cross product.
The transformation from world to view coordinates is achieved through two basic operations: translation and rotation.

key_terms.definition: 3D viewing transformation is the process of transforming a scene description from a 3D world coordinate description into a 3D view coordinate description. This transformation simulates the process of viewing a scene through a camera mechanism.

View coordinate system is a coordinate system that has its own axes (u, n, and v) and is used to represent the scene from the camera's perspective. This system is established based on the parameters of the camera.

Camera parameters are the specific values used to define the view coordinate system. These parameters include the camera position, the view of point, the view direction, and the center of interest or look-at point.

Composite transformation matrix is the matrix that results from the dot product of the rotation and translation matrices. This matrix is used to obtain a point in the view coordinate system from its corresponding point in the world coordinate system.
Orthogonal axes are three mutually perpendicular axes (N, V, and U) that are determined using camera parameters. These three axes together define the view coordinate system.

segments.subgoal: Differentiate between perspective and parallel projection and their required view volumes

key_points.text: The clipping process discards objects that fall outside the defined view volume before projection occurs.
Perspective projection uses converging projectors that meet at a center of projection, which provides realistic rendering.
Parallel projection uses parallel projectors, meaning the center of projection is considered to be at infinity.
The view volume for perspective projection is a frustum, while the view volume for parallel projection is a rectangular parallelepiped.

key_terms.definition: View plane is the 2D surface used as the target for projecting 3D objects from the view coordinate system. These planes are typically defined as a rectangular area, which is often called a clipping window.
Clipping window is a rectangular area that serves as the 2D view plane description onto which 3D objects are projected. This concept is often used interchangeably with the view plane itself.

View volume is a three-dimensional region within the scene that determines which portion of the scene will be projected onto the view plane. This volume defines the specific area of the scene that the system is intended to project.
Clipping process is the action of discarding objects that are part of the scene but fall outside of the defined view volume. This process occurs before the projection is performed.

Perspective projection is a type of projection where the lines, called projectors, emanating from the object converge toward a specific center of projection. This method is used to generate a realistic rendering and feeling in the scene.

segments.subgoal: Explain the use of canonical view volumes and projection matrices for rendering

key_points.text: Canonical view volumes simplify the computationally intensive process of clipping objects against complex view volumes.
For parallel projection, the canonical view volume is obtained by scaling the arbitrarily defined view volume.
For perspective projection, converting the frustum to a normalized unit cube requires both scaling and shearing operations.
Projection is performed by multiplying 3D point vectors by projection matrices, followed by dividing by the homogeneous factor w to obtain Cartesian coordinates.

key_terms.definition: Canonical view volume is a concept used to simplify pipeline computations in rendering. It involves converting any defined view volume, regardless of its shape or size, into a normalized cube.

Clipping operation is the process of discarding objects that are outside the defined view volume. When performed using the naive method, this requires computing the intersection of the view volume boundaries with the object boundaries.
Normalized cube is a standard cube used to define the view volume. It is the result of converting any arbitrary view volume into a standardized shape and size.

Parallel projection is a type of projection where the canonical view volume can be obtained by simply scaling the arbitrarily defined view volume. This method is computationally simpler than perspective projection.

Perspective projection is a type of projection that requires converting the frustum into a parallel canonical view volume, which is a normalized unit cube. This conversion involves both scaling and shearing operations.

segments.subgoal: Describe the sequence of transformations for projection and viewport mapping

key_points.text: The projection from world coordinates to the 2D view plane involves transforming the point to the view system, then to a canonical view volume, and finally projecting it onto the view plane.
The final point on the view plane is computed by multiplying the original world point P by a composite transformation matrix.
The 'window' is an abstract normalized clipping window, while the 'viewport' is a portion of the screen defined in device space.

review.question: How does perspective projection differ from other types of projection, and what visual quality does it achieve?
review.answer: In perspective projection, the lines (projectors) emanating from the object converge toward a single point, known as the center of projection. This convergence is what gives the scene a realistic feeling.

review.question: When using parallel projection, what is the relationship between the projectors, and where is the center of projection located?
review.answer: The projectors in parallel projection are parallel to each other. This means that the center of projection is conceptually located at infinity, so the lines never meet.

review.question: What specific geometric shapes are used for the view volume when employing perspective projection versus parallel projection?
